questions.question: What is the primary goal of database normalization?
options: To reduce data redundancy and improve integrity
questions.explanation: Normalization organizes data to minimize redundancy and dependency, improving data integrity.

questions.question: What is First Normal Form (1NF)?
options: All attributes depend on the key
questions.explanation: 1NF requires that all column values be atomic, meaning indivisible and single-valued.

questions.question: What does Second Normal Form (2NF) eliminate?
questions.explanation: 2NF removes partial dependencies where non-key attributes depend on part of a composite key.

questions.question: What does Third Normal Form (3NF) eliminate?
questions.explanation: 3NF eliminates transitive dependencies where non-key attributes depend on other non-key attributes.

questions.question: What condition must be met for a table to be in 2NF?
options: Must be in 1NF and have no transitive dependencies
Must be in 1NF and have no partial dependencies
Must have a composite primary key
questions.explanation: A table must first be in 1NF and then have all non-key attributes fully dependent on the entire primary key.

questions.question: What is a partial dependency?
options: A non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute
A non-key attribute depends on part of a composite key
All attributes depend on the whole key
A key depends on a non-key attribute
questions.explanation: A partial dependency exists when a non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite primary key.

questions.question: What is a transitive dependency?
options: A depends on B, and B depends on C
A non-key attribute depends on part of the key
All attributes depend on the primary key
Multiple tables depend on each other
questions.explanation: A transitive dependency occurs when a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute, which depends on the key.

questions.question: What normal form requires every non-key attribute to be non-transitively dependent on the primary key?
questions.explanation: Third Normal Form (3NF) requires elimination of transitive dependencies on the primary key.

questions.question: What is Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)?
questions.explanation: BCNF is a stricter version of 3NF where every determinant must be a candidate key.

questions.question: What process involves breaking a table into multiple tables?
questions.explanation: Decomposition splits a table into smaller tables to achieve higher normal forms and reduce redundancy.

questions.question: What is a functional dependency?
options: When two attributes always have the same value
When the value of one attribute uniquely determines the value of another
When a row is duplicated in a table
When a table has no primary key
questions.explanation: A functional dependency A → B means each value of A is associated with exactly one value of B.

questions.question: Which normal form eliminates non-trivial multi-valued dependencies?
questions.explanation: Fourth Normal Form requires every multi-valued dependency's determinant to be a superkey.

questions.question: Which normal form is also called Project-Join Normal Form (PJNF)?
questions.explanation: Fifth Normal Form is called PJNF because it deals with decomposition via projections and joins.

questions.question: What is an insertion anomaly?
options: Losing unrelated data when deleting a row
Being unable to insert data without adding unrelated data
Having to update the same fact in many rows
questions.explanation: An insertion anomaly occurs when a fact cannot be stored unless unrelated, sometimes unknown, data is supplied.

questions.question: What is an update anomaly?
options: Updating one row causes rows to be deleted
The same fact must be changed in multiple rows
New rows cannot be added to the table
questions.explanation: Update anomalies arise from redundancy: changing a fact requires updating every row that stores it.

questions.question: What is a deletion anomaly?
options: Rows cannot be deleted from a table
Deleting a row unintentionally loses unrelated facts
Deletion takes too long to execute
questions.explanation: A deletion anomaly occurs when removing one fact also removes unrelated data that should be kept.

questions.question: What is denormalization?
options: Removing all redundancy from a database
Intentionally adding redundancy to improve query performance
Splitting large tables into smaller ones
questions.explanation: Denormalization deliberately introduces controlled redundancy to reduce joins and speed up reads.

questions.question: What does the lossless join property guarantee?
options: Natural-joining the decomposed tables recreates the original data
All keys are preserved as primary keys
questions.explanation: A lossless decomposition lets the natural join of the fragments reconstruct the original relation exactly.

questions.question: What does dependency preservation mean in decomposition?
options: All dependencies are removed from the schema
Every original functional dependency can be enforced without joining tables
All tables are merged back together
Only primary key dependencies are kept
questions.explanation: Dependency preservation means each functional dependency can be checked within a single decomposed relation.

questions.question: What do we call a table that contains repeating groups or non-atomic values?
questions.explanation: A table with repeating groups or multi-valued cells is unnormalized (UNF or 0NF); it must be flattened to reach 1NF.

questions.question: A table in 1NF whose primary key is a single attribute automatically satisfies which normal form?
questions.explanation: With a single-attribute key, no non-key attribute can depend on just part of the key, so no partial dependency can exist.

questions.question: In the functional dependency X → Y, what is X called?
questions.explanation: The left-hand side of a functional dependency is the determinant; the right-hand side is the dependent.

questions.question: Which set of inference rules derives all functional dependencies implied by a given set?
questions.explanation: Armstrong's axioms — reflexivity, augmentation, and transitivity — are sound and complete for inferring FDs.

questions.question: What is a minimal set of functional dependencies equivalent to a set F called?
questions.explanation: A canonical (minimal) cover is the smallest set of FDs that implies all and only the dependencies of F.

questions.question: A table stores (StudentID, CourseID, CourseName) with key (StudentID, CourseID), where CourseName depends only on CourseID. Which normal form does it violate?
questions.explanation: CourseName depends on only part of the composite key — a partial dependency — violating 2NF.

questions.question: A table Employee(EmpID, DeptID, DeptName) has EmpID as the key, and DeptName depends on DeptID. Which normal form does it violate?
questions.explanation: DeptName depends on the non-key attribute DeptID — a transitive dependency — violating 3NF.

questions.question: Table Enrollment(StudentID, Course, Instructor) has key {StudentID, Course} and the dependency Course -> Instructor (each course has one instructor). What is the highest normal form the table satisfies?
questions.explanation: Instructor depends on only part of the composite key (a partial dependency), violating 2NF, so the table is only in 1NF.

questions.question: A relation is in BCNF if and only if which condition holds for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y?
options: Y must be a prime attribute
X must contain a foreign key
Y must be functionally dependent on every candidate key
questions.explanation: BCNF requires every determinant to be a superkey; 3NF relaxes this when the right side is a prime attribute.

questions.question: Why might a designer deliberately stop at a 3NF decomposition instead of pushing to BCNF?
options: The 3NF synthesis algorithm guarantees a lossless, dependency-preserving decomposition, which BCNF cannot always guarantee
questions.explanation: The 3NF synthesis algorithm preserves both losslessness and all functional dependencies; a BCNF decomposition may lose dependency preservation.

questions.question: For F = {A -> B, AB -> C, D -> AC, D -> E}, which attribute is extraneous in the left side of AB -> C?
questions.explanation: Since A+ under F already contains C (A -> B then AB -> C), removing B leaves A -> C still implied, so B is extraneous.

questions.question: A relation is in 3NF and has exactly one candidate key. Must it also be in BCNF?
options: Yes — a single key makes every determinant a superkey
Yes — 3NF and BCNF coincide for one-key relations
No — a non-superkey could still determine a prime attribute
No — 3NF relations are never in BCNF
questions.explanation: With exactly one candidate key, a non-superkey determinant X -> B where B is in the key would make X union (K minus B) a second candidate key, contradicting uniqueness; every determinant must be a superkey, so the relation is BCNF.
